about: Quick answer boxes on notes pages (scripts/lib/quick-answers.mjs, docs/quick-answers.md). One entry per page: q is the question a student would type into Google or ChatGPT; a answers it in two or three sentences using only facts the page itself teaches.

anatomy-physiology/notes/cardiac-cycle.h.q: What are the phases of the cardiac cycle?
anatomy-physiology/notes/cardiac-cycle.h.a: The cardiac cycle has five phases: ventricular filling, atrial contraction, isovolumetric contraction, ventricular ejection and isovolumetric relaxation. Valves open and close only because of pressure differences, so the mitral and aortic valves are both closed during the two isovolumetric phases. At 75 beats per minute one cycle lasts 0.8 second.

bio/notes/water-hydrogen-bonding.html.q: Why does water form hydrogen bonds?
bio/notes/water-hydrogen-bonding.html.a: Water is polar: its bonds between oxygen and hydrogen are polar and the molecule is bent, so the oxygen end carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogens partial positive charges. The partially positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the partially negative oxygen of a neighbor, and that attraction is a hydrogen bond. Each water molecule can hydrogen-bond with up to four neighbors.

chem/notes/math-units.html.q: How do you convert units with dimensional analysis?
chem/notes/math-units.html.a: Multiply by a conversion factor, a ratio such as 1000 m / 1 km that equals 1, with the unit you have on the bottom and the unit you want on the top so the old unit cancels. When no single factor connects two units, chain several: 4250 mg × (1 g / 1000 mg) × (1 kg / 1000 g) = 0.00425 kg. Then check the size: more of a smaller unit, fewer of a larger one.

ochem/notes/fischer.html.q: How do you tell R or S from a Fischer projection?
ochem/notes/fischer.html.a: Rank the four groups by CIP priority and trace 1 to 2 to 3: clockwise is R and counterclockwise is S. Then check the lowest priority group, usually H. Horizontal lines point toward you, so if it is on a horizontal line, flip the answer; vertical lines point away, so if it is on the vertical line, keep the answer as read.

ochem/notes/carbocations.html.a: Alkyl groups on the charged carbon stabilize it, so tertiary is most stable, then secondary, then primary, then methyl, mainly through hyperconjugation with a smaller effect from induction. Resonance helps more: a primary allylic cation is about as stable as a secondary alkyl one, and a primary benzylic cation about as stable as a tertiary one. Vinyl and aryl cations get no help from their π electrons.

anatomy-physiology/notes/action-potentia.q: What are the phases of an action potential?
anatomy-physiology/notes/action-potentia.a: An action potential has a rising phase, a falling phase and an afterhyperpolarization. At threshold, about −55 mV, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushing in drives the rise from rest at −70 mV to about +30 mV; then sodium channels inactivate and delayed potassium channels let potassium out. Potassium channels are slow to close, so the membrane dips to about −80 mV before returning to rest.

calculus/notes/math-functions.html.q: How do you find the domain of a function?
calculus/notes/math-functions.html.a: The domain is the set of inputs the rule accepts, and for the functions in this course two things shrink it: a denominator can never be 0, and a square root needs a number that is 0 or more. For example, h(x) = √(x + 4) / (x − 1) needs x + 4 ≥ 0 for the root and x − 1 ≠ 0 for the denominator, so its domain is x ≥ −4 and x ≠ 1.

anatomy-physiology/notes/anatomical-posi.a: The anatomical position is the reference posture used to describe every location in the body: standing upright and facing forward, feet flat and close together, arms hanging at the sides with the palms turned forward and the thumbs pointing away from the body. Every directional term describes the body as if it were in this position, whatever position it is really in.

anatomy-physiology/notes/erythrocytes.ht.q: What do red blood cells do, and how does their structure help?
anatomy-physiology/notes/erythrocytes.ht.a: Red blood cells carry oxygen bound to hemoglobin, and each hemoglobin molecule can carry four oxygen molecules. A red cell is a thin, flexible biconcave disc about 7.5 µm across, and because no point inside it is far from the membrane, oxygen diffuses in and out quickly. It has no nucleus or organelles, which leaves room for more hemoglobin, and it lasts about 120 days.

ochem/notes/energy-diagrams.html.q: What is the difference between a transition state and an intermediate on an energy diagram?
ochem/notes/energy-diagrams.html.a: A transition state is a peak on the energy diagram and an intermediate is a valley between two peaks. A transition state has bonds partly broken and partly formed and is not a compound you can put in a bottle, while an intermediate, such as a carbocation, is a real species with every bond fully made. Count the humps to count the steps.

anatomy-physiology/notes/connective-tiss.q: What are the types of connective tissue?
anatomy-physiology/notes/connective-tiss.a: Connective tissues fall into three groups: connective tissue proper (the loose and dense tissues), supportive connective tissue (cartilage and bone) and fluid connective tissue (blood). All have relatively few cells scattered through a large amount of extracellular matrix, made of ground substance plus fibers. The matrix, not the cells, gives each tissue its properties.

ochem/notes/grignard-reagents.html.q: What is a Grignard reagent and what does it react with?
ochem/notes/grignard-reagents.html.a: A Grignard reagent is a carbon nucleophile made by stirring an organic iodide, bromide or chloride with magnesium in dry ether, which slots the magnesium between the carbon and the halogen. It adds once to an aldehyde or ketone and twice to an ester, giving a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol after acidic workup. Any acidic proton in the flask, such as water, destroys it.

bio/notes/tonicity-osmoregulation.html.q: What is the difference between hypotonic, hypertonic and isotonic solutions?
bio/notes/tonicity-osmoregulation.html.a: Tonicity compares a solution with a cell: a hypotonic solution has fewer non-crossing solutes than the cell, so water moves in; a hypertonic one has more, so water moves out; an isotonic one has the same, so there is no net change. In a hypotonic solution an animal cell swells and may burst, while a plant cell becomes turgid.

ochem/notes/nucleophilic-aromatic.html.q: How does nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) work?
ochem/notes/nucleophilic-aromatic.html.a: SNAr is addition first, elimination second: the nucleophile adds to the carbon carrying the leaving group to form a negatively charged Meisenheimer complex, then the leaving group leaves and aromaticity returns. It needs strong electron-withdrawing groups such as nitro ortho or para to the leaving group, and fluorine is the best leaving group. With no withdrawing group, a very strong base gives benzyne instead.

ochem/notes/aromaticity.html.q: How do you know if a compound is aromatic?
ochem/notes/aromaticity.html.a: A ring is aromatic only if it meets all four requirements: it is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated (every ring atom has a p orbital in the loop) and holds 4n + 2 π electrons, such as 2, 6, 10 or 14. The electron count is Hückel's rule. Benzene meets all four and is 36 kcal/mol more stable than an imaginary cyclohexatriene with three fixed double bonds.

anatomy-physiology/notes/cell-junctions..q: What are the three types of cell junctions?
anatomy-physiology/notes/cell-junctions..a: The three main types are tight junctions, desmosomes and gap junctions. Tight junctions seal the space between cells, desmosomes rivet cells together against pulling forces, and gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of neighboring cells so water, ions and small molecules pass between them.

ochem/notes/cis-trans-ez.html.q: What is the difference between cis/trans and E/Z?
ochem/notes/cis-trans-ez.html.a: On an alkene, cis and trans work only when each alkene carbon carries one hydrogen and one other group: same side is cis, opposite sides is trans. Where those words stop working, E/Z takes over: rank the two groups on each carbon by CIP priority, and the alkene is Z if the higher priority groups are on the same side and E if they are on opposite sides.

nremt/notes/airway-management.html.q: When do you use a jaw-thrust instead of a head-tilt/chin-lift?
nremt/notes/airway-management.html.a: Use the head-tilt/chin-lift by default, when no spinal injury is suspected, and the jaw-thrust when you suspect a spinal injury, because it opens the airway without moving the neck. If the jaw-thrust does not open the airway, use the maneuver that does, because an open airway outranks spinal precautions.

physics/notes/math-units.html.q: How do you convert units in physics?
physics/notes/math-units.html.a: Multiply by a fraction whose top and bottom are equal, such as (1 m / 100 cm), with the unit you want on top and the unit you want to get rid of on the bottom, then cancel units. For example, 72 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 20 m/s. Convert every value to meters, kilograms and seconds before you put it into an equation.

ochem/notes/atomic-structure.html.q: What are valence electrons and the octet rule?
ochem/notes/atomic-structure.html.a: Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost occupied shell, the only ones that take part in bonding: carbon has 4, nitrogen 5 and oxygen 6. The octet rule says an atom is most stable with a full outer shell, which is 8 electrons for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and the halogens and 2 for hydrogen. An atom short of a full shell gains, loses or shares electrons to reach one.
